sections.title: Executive Summary
sections.content:
Welcome to the woods.

El Woods is a uniquely immersive retail + eco-cafe experience blending sustainability, art, and community. We're creating a space where walking through the door feels like stepping into the woods. Every aspect of the decor from the moment you walk in is curated to feel like a fully immersive woodland environment, creating a truly unique experience. Picture this: curated buy-sell-trade fashion, locally roasted coffee, baked goods from neighborhood bakeries, rotating art from local creators, open mic nights, community workshops. All wrapped in an environment of living walls, reclaimed wood, and natural light filtering through greenery. It's retail that feels like an escape.

But it's more than an escape, it's a response to a crisis.

The fashion industry consumes enough water annually to provide clean drinking water to 5 million people. A single cotton T-shirt requires 2,700 liters, which is what one person drinks in 2½ years. Every five minutes, 10,000 items hit the landfill. Textile waste accounts for 20% of global water pollution. Fast fashion isn't just wasteful. It's unsustainable.

We can't solve fast fashion and hyper-consumerism overnight. But we can offer better alternatives, and that starts with more than just selling used clothes. Thrift stores already do that. El Woods creates a space designed to shift mindsets, where eco-conscious consumption feels aspirational, not sacrificial. Our curated buy-sell-trade model isn't just about extending the life of garments, it's about reinforcing that you don't need more, you need better, and better doesn't have to mean new.

Denver ranks fourth nationally for secondhand stores per capita, but the good ones are generally clustered in RiNo, Capitol Hill, South Broadway. Wheat Ridge and the surrounding communities are totally underserved. Our target customers live there: eco-conscious millennials earning $50K-$100K who want what we're building but don't want to drive 30 minutes to find it.

And the timing is perfect. The global secondhand market is headed toward $350 billion by 2028. Denver's Waste No More ordinance shows where the city is going. We're riding the wave at exactly the right moment.

Year 1 revenue projection: $150K-$180K. Year 2: $220K-$280K. Clothing drives 65% of revenue at 60-70% margins. The cafe pulls 30%, and more importantly, it brings people through the door every single day. That's something pure retail just can't do.

Who We Are

Morgan McIntosh has spent 14+ years in retail, fashion, and customer experience. She knows how to create spaces people want to be in and experiences they actually remember. Ben Tyson is a serial entrepreneur with multiple exits and the operational brain that keeps the dream grounded. We're also married, which means we're all in on this. Together.

The Bigger Picture

El Woods is designed to grow beyond a single location. Year 2 brings El Woods Marketplace, an online platform for sustainable vendors, local artisans, and curated vintage. The physical store proves the concept. The marketplace scales it.

What We're Asking For

We're raising $100K-$125K to open a 2,000-3,000 sq ft location in Wheat Ridge. We're open to equity, convertible notes, revenue-based financing, or loans. What matters more than structure is alignment. We're looking for partners who believe sustainable business can be beautiful, profitable, and genuinely fun to build.

If normal is what you're after, there are plenty of options out there. We're building something different.

What We Learned

  • People will pay for quality curation. Our average transaction of $50-$75 proves customers value what we're doing.
  • Women's clothing with accessories drives the strongest sales. Our product mix is right.
  • The experience matters. Customers respond to our aesthetic, our story, our vibe. They get it.

Momentum We're Building

We're not waiting for the store to open to build community. We're growing @elwoods.revival with behind-the-scenes content, connecting with local artists and sustainable designers, and building inventory through ongoing buy appointments. By the time we open, people will already know who we are.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
The fashion industry has a massive waste problem. Let's look at the numbers:

U.S. Textile Waste

Water Pollution

People know this is a problem. They want to do better. But the current options aren't exactly inspiring.

Thrift Stores Need a Revival

Traditional thrift stores serve a purpose, but let's be honest: they're overwhelming, cluttered warehouses where finding something good feels like work. The experience is purely transactional. No connection. No community. No joy.

Even the chain buy-sell-trade stores like Buffalo Exchange operate as basic resale outlets. Better than Goodwill, sure, but they're not changing anyone's relationship with consumption. They're not making sustainable shopping feel like something you actually want to do.

That's the gap we're filling. A fundamentally different approach that makes secondhand shopping feel like a treat, not a compromise.

sections.title: The Experience
sections.content:
This is what makes El Woods different. Not just what we sell, but how it feels to be here.

Walk In and You're Somewhere Else

The moment you step through the door, something shifts. The air smells like coffee and something green, something alive. Living walls climb toward the ceiling, lush with ferns and trailing plants. Warm light filters through the greenery, dappled like sunlight through a forest canopy. The furniture is reclaimed wood, smooth from years of use, with a story you can feel. Soft ambient sounds play in the background. Not music, exactly. More like the feeling of being outside.

You're not in a store. You're in a world.

What You'll Find

The clothing racks aren't crammed. They're curated. Quality over quantity, always. Vintage gems hang next to eco-conscious contemporary pieces and work from local sustainable designers. Every item has been hand-selected for style, condition, and character. The hunt for something unique becomes part of the pleasure.

There's a cafe tucked into the corner. Locally roasted coffee, artisan teas, pastries from neighborhood bakeries. People linger here. They grab a latte and browse. They meet friends. They stay longer than they planned.

The walls rotate with work from local artists. There's an open mic Thursday nights. Sustainability workshops. Book swaps. Community events that give people reasons to come back, to connect, to belong.

How It All Works

Our buy-sell-trade model keeps clothing in circulation instead of landfills. Bring us your pre-loved pieces, and we'll pay you cash or store credit. Those items find new homes. It's a closed loop that generates inventory, drives repeat visits, and feels good for everyone involved.

By placing us in a living situation where we are seeing and feeling and being in the earth, it shapes our thinking, shapes our attitudes, and shapes our future.

"We're not just another thrift store with better lighting. We're creating a place people genuinely want to be."

sections.title: Market & Customers
sections.content:
Denver is one of America's most sustainability-conscious cities. It ranks fourth highest per capita for vintage and secondhand stores. The culture is here. People are already shopping sustainably. What's missing? An elevated, experiential destination in Wheat Ridge.

Why Wheat Ridge

All the good curated sustainable retail is concentrated in RiNo, Capitol Hill, and South Broadway. That's a 20-30 minute drive for people living in Wheat Ridge, Arvada, Golden, and Lakewood. These communities are growing, environmentally conscious, and totally underserved.

Wheat Ridge alone has 32,200 residents with a median income of $87,598. Arvada adds 123,000 more at $113,396. These are outdoor-loving, values-driven people who want what we're building. They just shouldn't have to drive across town to find it.

Our People

We're targeting millennials and young professionals, ages 25-35, household income $50K-$100K. But more than demographics, we're looking for a vibe. People who are eco-conscious without being preachy. Creative and artistic. They value unique style over fast fashion. They show up for local events. They want community and connection.

Right now, these customers shop curated vintage boutiques when they can get to them. They supplement with Goodwill when they can't. They browse Poshmark and Depop on their phones. They're willing to pay for quality and uniqueness. They just need somewhere convenient that feels worth the trip.

The Curious Newcomer

Beyond our core customer, we want to welcome people who are new to sustainable fashion entirely. For them, El Woods is an inviting entry point. A space where shopping consciously feels aspirational, not judgmental. Our immersive environment does the work. No lectures required.

sections.content:

Buy-Sell-Trade Clothing

The heart of El Woods. We buy pre-loved items from customers at 30-40% of resale value, curate for quality, and sell at accessible prices. The selection rotates constantly. There's always something new.

Pricing tiers:

  • Accessible basics: $15-$30
  • Quality mid-range: $30-$60
  • Premium vintage: $60-$100+

We also showcase local sustainable designers through consignment (30-40% commission on sales). Variety without inventory risk while supporting makers.

The Cafe

Locally roasted coffee ($4-7), artisan teas ($5-8), baked goods from neighborhood bakeries ($3-6). Compostable everything. Zero-waste as close as we can get.

But the cafe isn't just revenue. It's a traffic driver. Coffee customers come daily. Some browse. Some buy. All of them experience the brand. That's something pure retail can't do.

Community & Events

Open mic nights, sustainability workshops, art walks, book swaps. A rotating gallery of local artists (we take 20-30% commission). Ticketed events and private gatherings.

These activities generate some direct revenue, but their real value is deeper. They create belonging. Reasons to return. Social content and word-of-mouth. And they attract staff who want to work somewhere meaningful.

sections.title: Operations
sections.content:
Tuesday through Sunday, 10am-7pm (11am-5pm Sundays). Mondays are for inventory, admin, and buy appointments.

The Team

Morgan leads creative direction, merchandising, and the buy-sell-trade operation. Ben handles business ops, finances, and vendor relationships. We'll hire 2-3 part-time staff ($15-$18/hour) for barista and sales floor coverage.

A Day at El Woods

Mornings start with the cafe. Fresh coffee brewing, pastry case stocked. While the espresso machine warms up, we refresh clothing displays and process new inventory. By 10am, doors open.

Afternoons are peak hours. The lunch crowd comes for coffee and stays to browse. Buy-sell-trade appointments bring in new pieces. This is when the space comes alive: customers discovering finds, lingering over lattes, artists dropping by to check their work in the gallery.

Evenings wind down retail while setting up for events. On open mic Thursdays, the space transforms into something more. A gathering place, not just a store.

Inventory

Clothing comes from buy appointments, walk-in trades, estate sales, and occasional wholesale vintage. Everything gets quality-checked, photographed, priced, and tagged. Items that don't sell in 60-90 days get marked down or donated. We keep the floor fresh.

Cafe inventory is simple. Coffee weekly from our local roaster. Baked goods daily from a neighborhood bakery. No baking operation for us to manage.

Programming

Open mic every Thursday. Art walks bi-weekly. Monthly workshops and book swaps. Quarterly seasonal parties. This rhythm gives people reasons to come back. It creates the social fabric that makes El Woods more than a store.

sections.title: Marketing
sections.content:
Grassroots by design. Organic channels, community connections, word-of-mouth. This approach fits our budget, aligns with our values, and creates authentic engagement that paid media can't replicate.

"Fuck normal, I want magic."

Instagram First

Our home base is @elwoods.revival. Behind-the-scenes content, featured finds, artist spotlights, event promotion. Moody forest vibes, earthy tones, consistent with the in-store experience. We're building community before we even open the doors.

Partnerships

We're tapped into Denver's creative community: local artists, sustainable businesses, coffee roasters, bakeries, environmental orgs. These relationships create natural co-marketing. Rotating gallery shows. Cross-referrals. Collaborative events. Everyone benefits.

Launch Plan

8-12 weeks pre-launch: tease the buildout on Instagram, collect emails, announce partnerships. Launch week: grand opening party with live music and local artists, early access for founding members, press outreach to Westword, 5280, Denver Post.

After that, marketing is community programming. Weekly events drive content and traffic. Customer spotlights keep the feed authentic. The experience markets itself.

Budget

$3,000-$5,000 for launch. $500-$1,000/month ongoing. Emphasis on organic and earned media. We're investing in events that drive community, not ad spend.

sections.title: Mission & Impact
sections.content:
Profit isn't the only point. Our model creates measurable positive impact, not as marketing, but as core to who we are.

Impact Through Operations

Every piece of clothing we sell is one diverted from a landfill. Every item we buy stays in circulation. That's not a donation line item. It's built into every transaction.

Year 1 GoalsTarget
Clothing items diverted from landfill3,000+
Pounds of textiles saved2,500+ lbs
Water saved vs. new production8+ million liters

Compostable cups and packaging. Reusable bags. Reclaimed wood in the build-out. Aligned with Denver's Waste No More ordinance because it's who we are.

The Giveback Pledge

Once we reach profitability, 5-10% of net proceeds goes to environmental causes. Year 2 goal: $10,000+. Year 3: $20,000+. We're being intentional about the timeline. Better to build a strong foundation and give consistently for decades.

Where It Goes

Wildfire prevention and recovery. Colorado has seen devastating fires: Marshall, Cameron Peak, countless others. This is local and personal. We'll support prevention programs, forest restoration, and community recovery.

Deforestation awareness. Reforestation partnerships, educational programming, tree-planting initiatives. The forest theme isn't just aesthetic. It's a reminder of what we're fighting for.

Community

Local artists get free gallery space (70-80% of sales go to them). Sustainable designers access our consignment program. We host workshops, talks, and youth programs. We're not just selling clothes. We're building a community around environmental stewardship.
